title: Circles, Not Screens: Relationships in a Digital Classroom
tagline: Teachers sit in a real community circle about group chats, AI companions, and sleep, then plan their own circle, co-create agreements, and rehearse what to say when a student tells them something online went wrong.
groupSize: One circle of up to 16, or several circles of 8–12 with a keeper each; triads for the rehearsal
overview: Students' social lives now run through group chats, games, shared photos, and, for some, AI companion chatbots, yet those lives rarely come into the classroom until something goes wrong. A community circle is a simple, device-free structure that makes space to talk about online life before it becomes a crisis. In this session, teachers first sit in a circle as students, then choose and adapt grade-level prompts, turn the circle's needs into agreements, and rehearse the first two minutes after a student discloses a problem online. They leave with a planned first circle and a short note that invites families into the conversation.
objectives: Participants will experience and name the parts of a community circle (opening, check-in, core rounds, closing) and the keeper's moves that make it feel safe.

Participants will select and adapt circle prompts about online life for their grade band so every student can participate, including students who pass, are new to English, or have little device access at home.
Participants will rehearse a supportive, policy-aligned response to a student's disclosure that something online went wrong.
Participants will plan a first circle and draft a family note that invites households to share their own technology agreements.

print: Handout A: Circle Prompt Cards (1 set per table, cut apart; print the facilitator notes on a separate sheet)
Handout B: When a Student Tells You (1 per person)
Handout C: My First Circle Planner (1 per person)
A talking piece (a soft ball, a smooth stone, or any object that is easy to pass)
Chart paper titled "What we need from each other"; markers
Your campus's reporting procedure for student safety concerns and your counselor's name and contact (bring it or look it up before the session)
digital: None required. Optional: a shared document or slide where each person posts their finished planner and family note after the session

prep: Arrange chairs in a circle with no tables in the middle. If you have more than 16 people, set up several circles and ask a volunteer in each to be the keeper after you model it once.
Print and cut Handout A; sort the cards by grade band so tables can grab the set that matches them.
Find your district's or campus's procedure for reporting student safety concerns and the counselor contacts. Participants will write these into Handout C, so the rehearsal ends with a real next step.
Read the four scenarios on Handout B and decide which one you'll model. Scenario 3 (the shared photo) is the one participants find hardest; save it for the triads.

steps.title: Open the circle
steps.body: Welcome people into the circle without explanation. Hold up the talking piece: "Only the person holding this talks. Everyone else listens. You can always pass." Go first and model a short, honest answer to: **"Name one place, online or off, where you feel most like yourself."** Pass the piece to your left and let it go all the way around.
steps.note: Going first, briefly and a little vulnerably, is the keeper's most important move. It sets the length and the tone. Don't comment on answers; a nod is enough.

steps.title: Sit in a circle as students
steps.body: Run a short circle exactly as you would with middle schoolers. **Check-in:** "If your week so far were weather, what would it be?" **Core round:** "What's one thing group chats do well, and one thing they do badly? Don't use anyone's name." **Second core round:** "Some people talk to AI chatbots when they're bored, stressed, or lonely. Why might someone do that? What can a chatbot not give you that a person can?" **Closing:** "One word for how you're leaving." Then step out of role and ask: "What did I do as the keeper that made that feel safe, or not?" Chart the moves: going first, allowing pass, third-person framing, no fixing, no follow-up questions in the circle.
steps.note: Look for: participants noticing that the "don't use anyone's name" and "why might *someone*" framing let people talk about real experiences without exposing anyone. That framing is what makes online-life topics safe for a whole class.

steps.title: Choose and adapt prompts for your grade
steps.body: Tables take the Handout A set for their grade band. Each person chooses **three prompts** they'd use in the first month and **adapts one** so every student can join: simpler language or a visual choice for younger students, a sentence frame or home-language option for emergent bilinguals, a version that doesn't assume a phone or internet at home, a gesture or card to hold up for students who don't want to speak. Share one adaptation with a neighbor and explain who it welcomes in.
steps.note: Common misconception: that circle prompts must be about feelings to count. Prompts about games, shows, and group chats build the relationship that makes the feelings conversation possible later.

steps.title: From needs to agreements
steps.body: Pass the talking piece once more with: **"What do you need from this group to talk honestly about online life?"** Scribe answers on the "What we need from each other" chart. As a group, turn the needs into four or five agreements in student-friendly language, for example "What's said in circle stays in circle, unless someone might get hurt" and "We talk about what happened, not who did it." Point out that the first agreement includes the limit of confidentiality. Students need to hear it before anyone discloses anything.
steps.note: If your class already has digital-space norms, link them: circle agreements are about how we talk *here*; digital norms are about how we treat each other *there*. Students should notice they're the same values.

steps.title: Rehearse: when a student tells you
steps.body: Read the response moves on Handout B aloud, then model Scenario 1 with a volunteer playing the student. Triads rotate roles (student, teacher, observer) through Scenarios 2–4, **three minutes per round plus one minute of observer feedback**. The observer listens for the moves: thank them, listen without interrogating, don't promise secrecy, don't ask to see or receive images, say what happens next, and follow the campus procedure. After the rounds, each person writes their campus contact and procedure into Handout C.
steps.note: The hardest move for caring adults is *not* fixing it on the spot, especially not by confronting other students or asking to see the evidence. Your role is to keep the student safe, report through the right channel, and keep the relationship intact.

steps.title: Plan your first circle and a family bridge
steps.body: Using Handout C, each person plans a 15-minute first circle: when it happens, the opening, the check-in, one adapted core prompt, the agreements, and the closing. Then they draft a **three-sentence family note** that tells families what the class will talk about, invites them to share one technology agreement from their own home, and offers a non-digital way to respond (a paper slip, a phone call, a conversation at pickup). Close the whole session with one last round: "One thing you'll try in your first circle."
steps.note: Families are partners here, not an audience. A note that asks what *their* household agreements are respects different family rules and gives you insight into students' lives outside school.

unplugged: This session is fully unplugged by design: chairs, a talking piece, cards, chart paper, and printed planners. The subject is students' digital lives, but the practice is face-to-face, which is exactly the point. Family notes can go home on paper, with a tear-off reply slip.
digital: For a virtual session, use gallery view and a posted speaking order in place of the talking piece, and let people type "pass" in the chat. Use breakout rooms of three for the rehearsal and post Handout B on screen. Afterward, participants can post their planners and family notes to a shared folder so colleagues can borrow prompts. Keep student circles themselves in person and device-free; never record a student circle.
whyTech: This one is better unplugged. The point is to give students a place where their online lives can be talked about without a screen between people, and recording or typing would make disclosure less safe.

adaptations.label: K–2
adaptations.text: Keep circles to 10 minutes, use picture cards for the check-in (sun, cloud, rain, rainbow), and keep online-life prompts about screens they enjoy and how they know when to stop. Teach "tell a grown-up" as the circle's safety agreement.

Invite students to co-keep the circle after the first few weeks, and add prompts about sleep, pressure to always be reachable, and what they wish adults understood. Students may prefer to write a prompt anonymously on a card before it's used.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Offer sentence frames ("I feel ___ because ___"), accept answers in any language with a partner restating if the student wants, and make pass a fully respected choice.

adaptations.label: Librarians
adaptations.text: Run circles with classes that visit the library around book characters' online lives, then connect to digital citizenship lessons. Share your prompt set with the counselor so the language matches campus supports.

lookFors: Participants can name at least three keeper moves (going first, allowing pass, third-person framing, not fixing in the circle) and explain what each one protects.
Each adapted prompt on Handout C names which students it welcomes in and how (language, access, mode of response).
In the rehearsal, observers hear the teacher avoid promising secrecy, avoid asking to see images, and name a real next step with a real contact.
Family notes invite a two-way response and include at least one non-digital way to reply.
reflection: What strategies am I using to build positive relationships with my students, including around their lives online? (Teacher ELE 4.0)
Which students in my class are least likely to tell an adult when something online goes wrong, and what would make them more likely to?
How am I creating an environment where students with different home rules about technology all feel respected? (Teacher ELE 3.0)
transfer: Run your first circle within two weeks and send the family note home the same week. Bring back one thing that surprised you about students' online lives (no names) and one prompt you'd change.

handouts.title: Circle Prompt Cards
handouts.instructions: Cut apart and sort by grade band. The backs are facilitator notes on what to listen for; print them on a separate sheet.

cards.label: K–2 · Check-in
cards.front: If your feelings today were weather, what would they be? You can point to a picture.
cards.back: A universal opener. Picture cards let every child answer, including students who are new to English or not ready to talk.

cards.label: K–2 · Balance
cards.front: Tell about something fun you did on a screen, and something fun you did with no screen at all.
cards.back: Listen for balance, not rules. Families have different screen rules; never compare or praise one home's rules over another's.

cards.label: 3–5 · Connection
cards.front: What's a game or show you like, and who do you like to enjoy it with?
cards.back: Builds connection. If a student mentions an online-only friend they've never met who asks them for things, check in privately afterward, not in the circle.

cards.label: 3–5 · Balance
cards.front: How do you know when it's time to put a device down? What helps you stop?
cards.back: Students often name a person (a parent, an older sibling) or a routine. Gather their strategies; they're more persuasive to peers than yours.

cards.label: 6–8 · Group chats
cards.front: What's one thing group chats do well, and one thing they do badly? Don't use anyone's name.
cards.back: Listen for exclusion, screenshots shared without permission, and pile-ons. The no-names rule is what keeps this safe for a whole class.

cards.label: 6–8 · Tone
cards.front: Have you ever seen a message get taken the wrong way? What happened next?
cards.back: Opens the idea that tone disappears in text. Good bridge to co-creating norms for class discussion boards.

cards.label: 6–12 · AI companions
cards.front: Some people talk to AI chatbots when they're bored, stressed, or lonely. Why might someone do that? What can a chatbot not give you that a person can?
cards.back: Keep it in the third person and don't shame anyone. Students may say a chatbot is always available and never judges. Honor that, then ask what a friend or trusted adult can do that it can't.

cards.label: 9–12 · Sleep
cards.front: What does sleep compete with in your life? What's one thing that has helped you protect it?
cards.back: Avoid lecturing. Students' own strategies (charging a phone outside the room, a group-chat curfew) carry weight. Note who seems exhausted and check in privately.

cards.label: 9–12 · Being understood
cards.front: What's one thing you'd want an adult to understand about your online life that adults usually get wrong?
cards.back: Listen, don't defend. This prompt gives you the most useful information you'll get all semester about students' lives.

cards.label: All grades · Belonging
cards.front: Who is someone, online or offline, who makes you feel like you belong? What do they do?
cards.back: Surfaces what belonging looks like to your students. Their answers are a checklist for your own classroom.

cards.label: All grades · Home
cards.front: What's a rule about technology in your home that you think makes sense? You can pass.
cards.back: Honors different family norms. Some students have no device rules and some have no devices; welcome both without comment.

cards.label: All grades · Closing
cards.front: One word for how you're leaving the circle.
cards.back: Always close. A closing round signals the end of sharing and helps students transition back to academic work.

handouts.title: When a Student Tells You
handouts.instructions: Read the response moves, then rehearse the scenarios in triads. Everything here sits inside your district's policies; your campus procedure always comes first.
paragraphs: **The response moves.** (1) **Thank them:** "I'm really glad you told me." (2) **Listen without interrogating.** Let them tell it their way; ask only what you need to understand whether they are safe. (3) **Don't promise secrecy.** "I can't keep this just between us, because my job is to keep you safe, but I'll tell you who I'm talking to." (4) **Don't ask to see, receive, or save images or messages**, especially any image of a student. Note what they told you in their words. (5) **Say what happens next** and when you'll check back. (6) **Follow your campus procedure the same day:** your counselor, an administrator, and, where abuse or danger is involved, your legal duty as a mandated reporter.

**What not to do.** Don't confront the other students involved, don't take the student's phone, don't post about it, and don't handle a safety concern alone because it seems small. Small often turns out not to be.

**Scenario 1 (modeled by the facilitator).** A fourth grader lingers after circle: "Someone in my game keeps asking where I live. They said they're 11 but they talk like a grown-up. I didn't tell them. Am I in trouble?"

**Scenario 2.** A seventh grader says quietly: "There's a group chat where people are making fun of Jaylen's voice. I'm in it. I didn't say anything, but I didn't leave either. I feel gross about it."
**Scenario 3.** A tenth grader, upset: "Someone shared a photo of me from a sleepover. It's embarrassing, and now it's everywhere. Can you just look at it and tell me how bad it is?"
**Scenario 4.** An eighth grader after the AI-companion prompt: "Honestly the chatbot is the only one I really talk to. It gets me more than people do. It's fine, it's not a big deal."

**Observer look-fors.** Did the teacher thank the student? Stay calm and listen? Avoid promising secrecy? Decline to view the image in Scenario 3 while staying warm? Name a real next step and a real person? Leave the student feeling it was right to tell?

**After the rehearsal, write down:** who you contact on your campus, how you reach them, and what your district's procedure says to document. If you don't know, finding out is your first transfer task.

handouts.title: My First Circle Planner
handouts.instructions: Plan a 15-minute circle you'll run in the next two weeks, then draft the note that goes home.

Opening and check-in prompt (and how you'll go first):
One core prompt about online life, adapted. Who does your adaptation welcome in, and how (language, visual, no-device option, a non-speaking way to answer)?
Four or five circle agreements in student language, including the limit of confidentiality:
